subject: english
title: GCSE English Language diagnostic
curriculum: DfE GCSE English language subject content (2013), shared by AQA, Edexcel, OCR and WJEC. Also suitable for IGCSE. Literature set texts are not tested.

skills.name: Finding information
skills.why: Picking out the right details quickly is the first step in every reading question.
skills.strong: {name} reads carefully and picks out exactly the right details.
skills.developing: {name} finds most details but sometimes misses one when a question asks for more than one thing.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet finding details in a text reliably. This is the foundation of every reading question, so it comes first.
skills.next_step: We will practise close reading and checking each answer against the text.

skills.name: Inference and understanding
skills.why: Working out what a writer suggests, not just what they say, is what lifts reading answers into the higher grades.
skills.strong: {name} reads between the lines well and understands what characters think and feel.
skills.developing: {name} understands the surface of a text but finds it harder to work out what is implied.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident working out what a text suggests. This skill carries a lot of marks, so it is worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will practise asking 'what does this tell us?' about small details, with lots of discussion.

skills.name: Language and structure
skills.why: Explaining how a writer creates effects is at the heart of the GCSE reading papers.
skills.strong: {name} spots writers' techniques and explains their effects clearly.
skills.developing: {name} can name techniques but finds it harder to explain their effect on the reader.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident explaining how writers use language and structure. These questions are worth the most marks, so they are a priority.
skills.next_step: We will use a simple method for every quotation: what it says, how it says it, and the effect.

skills.name: Writing and accuracy
skills.why: Half of GCSE English Language is writing, and accurate spelling and punctuation are marked throughout.
skills.strong: {name} writes accurately and creates a clear, vivid picture for the reader.
skills.developing: {name} writes with some good ideas but makes errors with punctuation or sentence control.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet writing accurately and with control. Writing is half of the English Language GCSE, so this is worth real focus.
skills.next_step: We will work on sentence control and punctuation alongside planning and vocabulary.

passages.title: The Last Ferry
passages.text:
The last ferry of the day was already late when Mira reached the harbour. Rain had been falling since lunchtime, not heavily, but with the patient stubbornness of a guest who has no intention of leaving. She pulled her hood lower and dragged her suitcase over the cobbles, its broken wheel clattering like a complaint.

The harbour was almost empty. A single gull stood on the railing, feathers flattened by the wind, watching her with one yellow eye as if she owed it money. Beyond the harbour wall the sea heaved and slumped, grey on grey, and somewhere out there, hidden in the mist, was the island where her grandmother lived.

Mira had not seen her grandmother for six years. She remembered a kitchen that smelled of bread and woodsmoke, a radio that was never switched off, and a laugh so loud it made the teacups shiver. But six years was a long time. People changed. Letters had become shorter, then rarer, then stopped altogether.

A horn sounded, low and mournful, and the ferry slid out of the mist. It was smaller than she had expected, its white paint peeling in long strips, its name, Morning Star, almost worn away. A man in a yellow coat threw a rope onto the quay and looked up at her.

"You'll be Agnes's girl," he said. It was not a question.

Mira nodded. Her mouth had gone dry.

"She's been down here every day this week," he said, lifting her suitcase with one hand as if it weighed nothing. "Asking if you'd come."

For the first time that afternoon, Mira noticed that the rain had almost stopped.

questions.stem: How long had it been raining when Mira reached the harbour?
questions.explain: Paragraph 1: 'Rain had been falling since lunchtime'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
questions.explain: The dog's tail: singular possession. 'It's' means 'it is'; 'its' never takes an apostrophe for possession.

questions.stem: What is the name of the ferry?
questions.explain: Paragraph 4: 'its name, Morning Star, almost worn away'.

questions.stem:
'Mira nodded. Her mouth had gone dry.'

How is Mira feeling at this moment?
questions.explain: A dry mouth is a physical sign of nerves. Nothing suggests boredom or anger.

questions.stem: How many years is it since Mira last saw her grandmother?
questions.explain: Paragraph 3: 'Mira had not seen her grandmother for six years.'

questions.stem:
'its broken wheel clattering like a complaint'

Which technique is used in this phrase?
questions.explain: A comparison using 'like' is a simile.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence:
'_____ going to miss the ferry if they don't hurry.'
questions.explain: They're = they are. 'Their' shows belonging; 'there' is a place.

questions.stem: Which TWO things does Mira remember about her grandmother's home?
options: A kitchen that smelled of bread and woodsmoke
A radio that was never switched off
questions.explain: Paragraph 3 mentions the smell of bread and woodsmoke and the radio. The other options are not in the text.

questions.stem:
'"You'll be Agnes's girl," he said. It was not a question.'

What does 'It was not a question' suggest?
options: The man already knew who Mira was
The man wanted to see her ticket
questions.explain: He states it as a fact: he has been expecting her, which links to the grandmother waiting every day.

questions.stem:
'Beyond the harbour wall the sea heaved and slumped, grey on grey'

What does the verb 'slumped' suggest about the sea?
options: It seems heavy and tired, making the scene feel gloomy
questions.explain: 'Slumped' suggests heaviness and weariness, adding to the bleak, grey mood.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semi-colon correctly?
options: The rain stopped; the sun came out.
The rain; stopped and the sun came out.
The rain stopped and; the sun came out.
questions.explain: A semi-colon joins two complete, closely related sentences.

questions.stem:
'Letters had become shorter, then rarer, then stopped altogether.'

What does this suggest about Mira and her grandmother?
options: They had argued about the letters
questions.explain: The gradual decline suggests they lost touch over time. No argument or move is mentioned.

questions.stem: The gull watches Mira 'as if she owed it money'. What is the effect of this detail?
options: It shows that gulls are dangerous
It shows that Mira is poor
It adds a touch of humour to a gloomy scene
It explains why the ferry is late
questions.explain: The comic image lightens an otherwise bleak description.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the ferry are true?
options: It was smaller than Mira had expected
questions.explain: Paragraph 4: 'smaller than she had expected' and 'white paint peeling'. It was late, and yellow is the man's coat.

questions.stem:
'For the first time that afternoon, Mira noticed that the rain had almost stopped.'

What does this final sentence suggest about how Mira feels now?
options: She is worried the rain will return
She is disappointed by the ferry
She feels calmer and more hopeful
questions.explain: After hearing her grandmother has been waiting, the easing rain mirrors her easing worry.

questions.stem: Why does the writer put 'Mira nodded. Her mouth had gone dry.' in its own very short paragraph?
options: To slow the pace and focus on her nerves at an important moment
To describe the setting in more detail
To show that a lot of time has passed
questions.explain: Isolating short sentences slows the pace and spotlights her reaction.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences contains a comma splice (two sentences wrongly joined by a comma)?
options: Mira was tired, so she sat down.
Mira was tired, she sat down.
Mira, who was tired, sat down.
Because Mira was tired, she sat down.
questions.explain: 'Mira was tired, she sat down' joins two main clauses with only a comma. It needs a full stop, semi-colon or conjunction.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between Mira and her grandmother, looking at the whole passage?
options: Close and unchanged since Mira was young
Unknown, because the grandmother has moved away
Distant, but the grandmother clearly still cares deeply
questions.explain: The letters stopped (distance), but the grandmother came to the harbour every day (care).

questions.stem: How does the writer use the weather across the whole passage?
options: The rain matches Mira's worries, and it stopping at the end suggests hope
The weather is only there to make the setting realistic
The rain shows that the ferry crossing will be dangerous
The weather gets worse to show Mira will be unhappy
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy: persistent rain mirrors her anxiety; the rain stopping mirrors her relief.

questions.stem:
Write the opening of a story set in a busy place, such as a market, a train station or a school canteen.

Write 6 to 10 sentences. Help the reader picture the scene. Spend about 8 minutes on this.

rubric.criterion: Vivid, precise vocabulary and at least one well-chosen technique (for example sensory detail or a simile) that helps the reader picture the scene
Clear organisation, with varied sentence openings and lengths
Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, with sentences correctly marked by full stops

questions.explain: Award each strand 0, 1 or 2. Two marks means the strand is secure throughout, one mark means it is partly there.
